Series::celu¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::celu(double alpha = 1.0) const
Series& Series::celu_() const
Series& Series::celu_(double alpha) const

Continuously Differentiable Exponential Linear Unit¶

celu() applies the continuously differentiable exponential linear unit elementwise:

celu(x, alpha) = x                              when x > 0
                 alpha * (exp(x / alpha) - 1)  otherwise

The positive branch is the identity. With positive alpha, the negative branch is exponential and approaches -alpha. Both branches meet at zero with value zero and slope one. That smooth join is the reason this operation exists: it retains an exponential negative response without introducing a derivative jump at the origin.

alpha controls both the negative saturation level and the curvature. The default gives exp(x)-1 on the non-positive side. A larger positive value makes that side less sharply curved. Zero is invalid because the formula divides by alpha; validation occurs before an output is returned. A finite negative value is evaluated by the same formula, although a positive value is the conventional activation contract.

The operation is out of place and preserves shape and platform. Floating input keeps its dtype. Integral input promotes to float32; the fractional negative branch is never truncated into integer storage.

Reverse Mode¶

For a tracked input, the local derivative is

1                 when x > 0
exp(x / alpha)    when x <= 0

The recorded derivative at zero is one. The backward path is represented as one activation node rather than exposing the comparison and exponential used to evaluate its branches.

In-Place Form¶

celu_() is the in-place sibling of celu(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

Despite being declared const at the call site — a quirk of how this method’s wrapper is generated, not a promise that self is left unchanged — celu_() genuinely mutates the series it’s called on.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-2.0, 0.0, 2.0});
x.celu_();
std::cout << x;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.86466472, 0, 2]

auto x = pluss::make_series({-2.0, 0.0, 2.0});
x.celu_(2.0);
std::cout << x;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.2642411, 0, 2]

Examples¶

Example 1. The default leaves positive values unchanged and bends negative values toward -1.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-2.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0}).celu());

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.8647, -0.6321, 0.0000, 1.0000, 2.0000]

Example 2. alpha=2 changes only the non-positive branch.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-2.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0}).celu(2.0));

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.2642, -0.7869, 0.0000, 1.0000, 2.0000]

Example 3. Rank and shape survive while integer input promotes.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({{-2, 0}, {1, 3}}).celu(0.5));

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float32, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ -0.4908 0.0000 ⎤
⎣  1.0000 3.0000 ⎦

Example 4. A sum objective reveals the elementwise derivative.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-2.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
x.celu(2.0).sum().reverse();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[0.3679, 0.6065, 1.0000, 1.0000]

Example 5. Zero alpha is rejected explicitly.

try {
  (void)pluss::make_series({-1.0, 1.0}).celu(0.0);
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  const std::string message = e.what();
  std::cout << message.substr(0, message.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

celu: expected alpha != 0

See Also¶

  • elu() exposes the general exponential-linear parameters.

  • selu() uses fixed self-normalizing coefficients.

  • relu() uses a hard zero branch instead of an exponential one.
